title: What is Databricks and how does it relate to Apache Spark — a unified data + AI platform built by Spark's creators, providing managed Spark clusters, collaborative notebooks, Delta Lake, and integrated ML/LLM tooling?

s1_definition.profdef: Databricks is a cloud-based unified data and AI platform created by the original authors of Apache Spark, which packages managed Spark clusters, collaborative notebooks, the Delta Lake storage layer, governance through Unity Catalog, and integrated machine learning and large-language-model tooling into one product. s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Databricks is a cloud-based unified data and AI platform created by the original authors of Apache Spark, which packages managed Spark clusters, collaborative notebooks, the Delta Lake storage layer, governance through Unity Catalog, and integrated machine learning and large-language-model tooling into one product. It relates to Spark as the commercial, managed, enhanced environment around open-source Spark: you still write Spark code, but Databricks runs it on an optimized Spark runtime and removes the burden of installing, configuring, scaling, and operating clusters yourself.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Apache Spark is a very powerful engine, like a bare jet engine sitting on a workshop floor. You could, with great effort, build your own aircraft around it, wire the controls, hire mechanics, and run the airport yourself. Databricks is like buying a complete, maintained aircraft from the people who designed that engine, with autopilot, a tuned version of the engine that runs faster, a cockpit where the whole crew works together, a secure cargo hold with an inventory system, and ground staff who handle fuelling and maintenance. At the National Bank of India you still decide where to fly and what cargo to carry, but you are not building and maintaining the plane and the airport; you focus on the journey.

**One line to remember:** Databricks is the managed, optimized, cloud platform around Apache Spark built by Spark's own creators, adding notebooks, Delta Lake, governance, and ML tooling so you run Spark without operating it.

sections.s2_technical:
Apache Spark is the open-source distributed compute engine, but using it in production means you also have to provision machines, install Spark, configure the cluster manager, tune memory, set up storage, manage libraries, secure it, and monitor it. Databricks was founded by the same people who created Spark to deliver all of that as a managed cloud service on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. When you run a job on Databricks you are still writing Spark, in PySpark, Scala, SQL, or R, but it executes on the Databricks Runtime, which is a performance-tuned distribution of Spark with extra optimizations such as the Photon vectorized engine, caching improvements, and tuned defaults, so the same code often runs considerably faster than on vanilla Spark.

Around the engine Databricks adds the pieces a data platform needs. Collaborative notebooks let multiple engineers and analysts write and run cells against a shared cluster, with visualizations and version history, which is how most interactive Databricks work happens. Delta Lake, also created by Databricks and open-sourced, is the default storage layer that brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and efficient upserts on top of Parquet files in cloud object storage, turning a raw data lake into a reliable lakehouse. Unity Catalog provides centralized governance: one place to manage access control, auditing, data lineage, and discovery across workspaces. Cluster management is automated, with autoscaling, auto-termination of idle clusters to save cost, and different cluster types for interactive versus production work. And the platform integrates machine learning end to end through managed MLflow for experiment tracking and model registry, feature stores, and increasingly large-language-model tooling for building generative AI applications on your own governed data.

A senior-level nuance is the lakehouse positioning: Databricks' thesis is that you no longer need a separate data lake and a separate data warehouse, because Delta Lake plus the Spark engine plus SQL endpoints give you both cheap raw storage and warehouse-style performance and reliability in one place. Another nuance is that Databricks is not a fork of Spark that locks you in at the code level; your Spark code is portable, and Delta Lake is open source, though features like Unity Catalog, the Photon engine, Delta Live Tables, and the managed services are Databricks-specific value you give up if you move off the platform. The practical point for a bank is that Databricks trades some cost and platform dependence for a very large reduction in operational effort, faster execution, strong governance which matters enormously in a regulated industry, and a single environment spanning ETL, analytics, and machine learning on the same governed data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the data team ran its own Spark clusters on bare virtual machines. They spent enormous time installing Spark, patching versions, tuning memory, fixing failed nodes, and babysitting clusters that were left running overnight and wasting money. Analysts could not easily collaborate, and there was no central control over who could see which sensitive tables. This is exactly the operational burden that a managed platform removes: the value is not writing different Spark code, it is not having to build and run the platform.

This is exactly how Databricks relates to Spark. You keep writing Spark, but the platform provisions tuned clusters on demand, autoscales them, auto-terminates idle ones to save cost, gives analysts shared notebooks, and enforces governance centrally.

Problem 2 — The team also had a split between a cheap raw data lake and an expensive warehouse, with brittle pipelines copying data between them and no reliable transactions on the lake. Adopting Delta Lake as the storage layer gave them ACID transactions and time travel directly on the lake, collapsing the two systems into one lakehouse. This is the lakehouse value that Databricks is built around.

Because we cannot run a real Databricks workspace here, this runnable demo models the platform's relationship to Spark conceptually. A `SparkEngine` represents the open-source compute. A `DatabricksRuntime` wraps it and adds a simulated performance boost, autoscaling, and auto-termination. A `ManagedWorkspace` hosts notebooks, a Delta-backed lakehouse with transactions and time travel, and a governance layer that checks access. The demo submits the same logical job to raw Spark and to the Databricks runtime to show the operational differences, then performs a governed, transactional Delta write with a time-travel read.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
databricks:
  runtime-version: "14.3-LTS"
  photon-enabled: true
  autoscale:
    min-workers: 2
    max-workers: 8
  auto-termination-minutes: 30
unity-catalog:
  enforce-access-control: true
```

Java source files:

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/databricks-platform-sim-1.0.0.jar com.bank.dbx.DatabricksDemo

# On real Databricks you simply write Spark in a notebook:

#   agg.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("trade_summary")

# Cluster provisioning, Photon, autoscaling, and governance are handled by the platform.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one logical Spark aggregation job of four hundred work units, and a sequence of governed notebook cells that ingest and write trades into a Delta table.

Step 1: The same aggregation job runs first on open-source Spark, which executes it at the baseline rate and logs that the team had to provision, tune, and monitor the cluster themselves.

Step 2: The same job runs on the Databricks runtime. The cluster auto-starts with the minimum workers, autoscales up based on the work size, and runs on the Photon-tuned engine, finishing in a fraction of the time, and the log shows the worker count and the speedup.

Step 3: After the job the runtime checks idle time against the auto-termination threshold and shuts the cluster down, which is how Databricks avoids paying for idle clusters overnight.

Step 4: In the lakehouse part, an authorized engineer runs an ingest notebook cell. Governance checks that the user is authorized, grants access, and runs the cell on the managed runtime.

Step 5: Two Delta writes commit, each creating a new atomic version of the trades table. The first commit adds two rows as version one, and the second adds a third row as version two, so the current table has three rows.

Step 6: A time-travel read asks for version one and gets back the two-row snapshot, demonstrating that Delta keeps historical versions. Finally an unknown contractor tries to run a cell that reads sensitive data, and the governance layer denies access, showing centralized access control.

Final output:


```
  ═══ LLD — Platform-over-Spark Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Decorator: DatabricksRuntime wraps SparkEngine, adds speed+ops     │

  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ SparkEngine   │◀───────│ DatabricksRuntime     │ (decorator)
  │ + runJob()    │ wraps  │ - photon, autoscale   │
  └──────────────┘        │ + runJob()            │
                          │ + autoTerminateIfIdle()│
                          └──────────┬────────────┘
                                     │ used by
                                     ▼
                          ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
                          │ ManagedWorkspace      │───────▶│ DeltaTable   │
                          │ - authorizedUsers     │ writes │ versions[]   │
                          │ + runNotebookCell()   │        │ + write()    │
                          └──────────────────────┘        │ + versionAsOf│
                                                           └──────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. SparkEngine.runJob("agg", 400) → 400s baseline
  2. DatabricksRuntime.runJob("agg", 400) → autostart, autoscale, Photon → 160s
  3. autoTerminateIfIdle(30,30) → cluster stopped
  4. ManagedWorkspace.runNotebookCell("rajesh", ...) → governance ✓
  5. DeltaTable.write(rows) → version 1, then version 2
  6. DeltaTable.versionAsOf(1) → historical snapshot
  7. runNotebookCell("unknown_contractor",...) → DENIED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Databricks is a cloud-based unified data and AI platform built by the original creators of Apache Spark, and the simplest way to describe the relationship is that Databricks is the managed, optimized, enterprise environment around open-source Spark. You still write Spark code in PySpark, SQL, Scala, or R, but it runs on the Databricks Runtime, which is a performance-tuned distribution of Spark with extra optimizations like the Photon vectorized engine, so the same code typically runs considerably faster, and you are freed from provisioning machines, installing and patching Spark, tuning memory, and babysitting clusters yourself.

Around the engine, Databricks adds the pieces a real data platform needs. Collaborative notebooks let engineers and analysts work together against shared clusters. Delta Lake, which Databricks created and open-sourced, is the default storage layer that brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and efficient upserts on top of Parquet in cloud object storage, turning a raw lake into a reliable lakehouse. Unity Catalog provides centralized governance, which means one place for access control, auditing, data lineage, and discovery, and that matters enormously in a regulated industry. Cluster management is automated with autoscaling and auto-termination of idle clusters to control cost, and the platform integrates machine learning end to end through managed MLflow, feature stores, and increasingly large-language-model tooling. The headline positioning is the lakehouse: the idea that you no longer need a separate lake and warehouse because Delta plus Spark plus SQL endpoints give you cheap storage and warehouse-grade performance and reliability in one place.

At the National Bank of India we moved off self-managed Spark on bare virtual machines, where the team burned time installing and patching Spark, fixing failed nodes, and paying for clusters left running overnight, and where analysts could not easily collaborate and there was no central control over sensitive tables. On Databricks the same Spark jobs ran faster on the tuned runtime, clusters autoscaled and auto-terminated to save money, analysts shared notebooks, and Unity Catalog gave us the governance the auditors required. Adopting Delta Lake also collapsed our brittle lake-plus-warehouse split into one lakehouse with real transactions and time travel on the lake. The honest trade-off I mention is cost and some platform dependence, because while your Spark code and Delta are open and portable, features like Photon, Unity Catalog, and the managed services are Databricks-specific, but in exchange you get far less operational effort, faster execution, strong governance, and one environment spanning ETL, analytics, and machine learning on the same governed data.
